Creationism
kree-AY-shuh-niz-um
n.
From creation + -ism; Latin creatio, from creare, to make, bring forth. In older theology the word also names the view that God creates each human soul directly (see Creationism of the Soul). In ordinary use it names the belief that God made the world as Genesis records it, against evolutionary naturalism.

Not to be confused: This entry is about the origin of the world. For the view that God creates each human soul directly, see Creationism (Origin of the Soul).

Definition · Webster 1828 · Scriptures · Corruption · Roots · Usage · Related

Biblical Definition

Creationism is the confession that the heavens, the earth, and everything in them were made by God, by His word, out of nothing, as Genesis 1–2 records. “In the beginning God created the heaven and the earth” (Genesis 1:1). The world was not drawn out of matter that was already there, and it was not produced by chance over unguided ages: “the worlds were framed by the word of God, so that things which are seen were not made of things which do appear” (Hebrews 11:3). The dictionary holds the plain reading of the text: six days of ordinary length, evening and morning, as the Fourth Commandment repeats: “in six days the LORD made heaven and earth, the sea, and all that in them is” (Exodus 20:11). Man did not rise from the beasts. God formed Adam from the dust and breathed life into him, then made Eve from his side, and those two are the historical parents of the whole race (Genesis 2:7; Genesis 2:22). Christ grounds marriage in that order: “from the beginning of the creation God made them male and female” (Mark 10:6). The 1689 Confession (4.1) says it pleased God to make the world and all things in it in the space of six days, and all very good. Creationism is not first a theory of geology. It is a confession about who owns the world and who owns the man: “thou hast created all things, and for thy pleasure they are and were created” (Revelation 4:11).

Webster 1828 Definition

Webster (1828) has no entry for creationism. He defines CREATION first as the act of causing to exist, and especially the act of bringing this world into existence, and cites Romans 1:20.

CREA’TION, n. 1. The act of creating; the act of causing to exist; and especially, the act of bringing this world into existence. Romans 1:20.

5. The things created; creatures; the world; the universe.

Key Scripture

Genesis 1:1 — "In the beginning God created the heaven and the earth."

Exodus 20:11 — "For in six days the LORD made heaven and earth, the sea, and all that in them is, and rested the seventh day: wherefore the LORD blessed the sabbath day, and hallowed it."

Hebrews 11:3 — "Through faith we understand that the worlds were framed by the word of God, so that things which are seen were not made of things which do appear."

Mark 10:6 — "But from the beginning of the creation God made them male and female."

Romans 1:20 — "For the invisible things of him from the creation of the world are clearly seen, being understood by the things that are made, even his eternal power and Godhead; so that they are without excuse:"

Revelation 4:11 — "Thou art worthy, O Lord, to receive glory and honour and power: for thou hast created all things, and for thy pleasure they are and were created."

Modern Corruption

The open corruption is evolutionary naturalism, which says the world made itself. The quieter one is theistic evolution, which keeps God’s name on the cover and lets Darwin write the chapters, and which cannot keep Paul’s Adam without rewriting Romans 5.

expand to see more

Naturalism teaches that matter, time, and chance account for everything, man included. Scripture does not treat that as a neutral finding. Paul says the things that are made show God’s eternal power and Godhead so plainly that men are left “without excuse” (Romans 1:20), and of those who would not glorify Him he says, “Professing themselves to be wise, they became fools” (Romans 1:22). The denial of the Creator is first a moral refusal and only afterward a theory. A man who will not have a Maker will not have a Lawgiver either.

Theistic evolution, sometimes called evolutionary creationism, keeps the Creator and hands the method to Darwin. Genesis 1–11 becomes poetry or myth. Adam becomes a population, or one hominid chosen out of many. Death, disease, and predation become the tools God used for millions of years before any man sinned. That cannot stand with the apostle. “By one man sin entered into the world, and death by sin” (Romans 5:12). If death was God’s method of making man, death is not the wages of sin, and the cross answers a problem God built into the world on purpose. Paul’s gospel needs a first Adam: “as in Adam all die, even so in Christ shall all be made alive” (1 Corinthians 15:22). Take away the first man and the second Adam has no one to stand for.

Not every departure weighs the same. Some Reformed men, Kuyper and Warfield among them, allowed an older earth while confessing a historical Adam, the fall, and inherited sin. The dictionary does not call that heresy, but it does not take that voice either: Exodus 20:11 ties the week a man works and rests to the week God worked and rested, and the plain reading is the faithful one. The word also has an older theological sense, the view that God creates each human soul directly, which is treated under Creationism of the Soul.

Greek & Hebrew Roots

The Hebrew bara’ is the verb of Genesis 1:1, and in its simple form Scripture never gives it any subject but God. Creation is His work alone.

expand to see more

Hebrew bara’ (H1254) — to create; in its simple stem used only of God

Hebrew yom (H3117) — day (evening and morning, Genesis 1)

Greek ktizō (G2936) — to create, found

Latin creare — to make, bring forth

Usage

"Creationism confesses that God made the heavens and the earth in six days and called it very good."

"He held to creationism not as a hobby of geology but as the ground of the Sabbath and of marriage."

"Creationism, the origin of the world, is distinct from creationism of the soul, the origin of each man’s soul."
